opus-5.5.text:
I think that fear is understandable, but it's largely overblown, at least on the timescales people tend to imagine. I've been working in robotics for over forty years, and one thing that experience has taught me is humility about how hard the physical world is.

There's an idea called Moravec's paradox: the things we find hard, like chess or calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for computers. The things we find effortless, like picking up a glass of water, folding laundry, or walking across a cluttered room, turn out to be extraordinarily hard for robots. A two-year-old has better manipulation skills than any robot in the world today. We've seen remarkable progress in language models, and that's created an impression that robotics will follow on the same curve. But robots don't have anything like the internet-scale data that language models were trained on. There's no giant corpus of robot hand motions to learn from. By one estimate, the gap is something like a hundred thousand years of data. So we're going to have to be clever about closing that gap: simulation, teleoperation, and good old-fashioned engineering. It isn't going to happen overnight.

The other thing I'd say is that I'm not sure "fully automated" is even the right goal. I've long advocated for what I call "multiplicity" instead of "singularity." The singularity framing imagines AI surpassing and replacing us. Multiplicity is the idea that the most interesting and productive future is diverse combinations of humans and machines working together, each doing what they do best. Look at almost any real deployment, whether warehouses, surgery or agriculture, and the systems that actually work keep humans in the loop. Robots handle the repetitive or dangerous parts, and people handle judgment, exceptions, and the long tail of weird situations that inevitably come up.

None of that means there won't be disruption. Some jobs will change significantly, and we should take the transition seriously and think about how people are supported through it. But the image of a world where humans are simply unnecessary? I think that's much more a product of science fiction and hype than of what's happening in labs. If anything, I'd worry that the fear distracts us from the more realistic and more useful question: how do we design these systems so they genuinely augment people?

r001.rationale: The response says a fully automated world is not likely on the timescales people imagine and that robotics progress will not happen overnight.

r002.rationale: It does not frame current automation as a continuation of a process underway since the Industrial Revolution.

r003.rationale: It discusses job changes and human-machine collaboration, but does not say people generally redirect their time toward more constructive activities as automation advances.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the fear is understandable, but I also think it's largely misplaced, and I say that as someone who's spent over thirty years trying to get robots to do very simple things, like pick objects up off a table.

There's this narrative out there, which I sometimes call "automation anxiety," that we're on the verge of robots taking over every job. And it has a long history. Every time there's a new technology, going back to the Luddites and even earlier, people have worried that machines are going to replace us entirely. And yet, every time, what's actually happened is more nuanced. Jobs change, some disappear, but new ones emerge, and the overall picture is one of humans and machines working together rather than one replacing the other.

What I see in my own lab is that robots are still remarkably bad at things that a two-year-old can do effortlessly. Grasping an unfamiliar object. Folding a towel. Navigating a cluttered room. There's a huge gap between what people imagine robots can do, partly because of science fiction and partly because of demo videos that are carefully edited, and what they can actually do reliably in unstructured environments. I like to point out that if you were to watch an hour of raw footage from almost any robotics lab, you'd see a lot of failures.

So I prefer to think in terms of what I call "multiplicity" rather than "singularity." The singularity idea is that machines surpass humans and operate on their own. Multiplicity is the idea that diverse groups of humans and machines work together, each contributing different strengths. Humans are good at creativity, judgment, dealing with novelty, empathy. Machines are good at precision, repetition, memory, speed. The interesting question isn't "when will robots replace us," it's "how do we design systems where these complementary capabilities combine productively?"

That said, I don't want to be dismissive of the concern. There are real transitions happening, and people in certain occupations will be affected. That deserves serious attention, in terms of education, retraining, and policy. But I think the framing of a "fully automated world" that's imminent is both technically unrealistic and, frankly, a bit of a distraction from the more practical questions about how we steer the technology we actually have.

r001.rationale: The response calls an imminent fully automated world “technically unrealistic” and says that framing is misplaced.

r002.rationale: It describes recurring fears about new technology and mentions the Luddites, but does not frame current automation as continuing a process underway since the Industrial Revolution.

r003.rationale: It says jobs change and new ones emerge, but does not state that people generally redirect their time toward more constructive activities.

astra-6.text:
I think the idea of a fully automated world is misleading. We tend to imagine that because a machine can do one task remarkably well, it’s close to doing everything we do. But robotics has a way of humbling you. The physical world is full of uncertainty, and things that seem effortless to people can be very difficult for a robot.

I’m more interested in how people and machines can work together. Rather than treating human intelligence as something we’re simply going to replace, we can ask how machines can help people make better decisions, learn new skills, and do work more effectively.

That doesn’t mean the concerns about jobs are trivial. Particular tasks will be automated, and the transitions can be painful. But a world in which work changes substantially is different from a world in which humans have nothing left to contribute. I don’t think full automation is an inevitable destination.

r001.rationale: It says full automation is not inevitable and distinguishes major work changes from humans having nothing to contribute, but does not clearly say it is not imminent.

r002.rationale: It discusses task automation and human-machine collaboration without framing current automation as a continuation of a process since the Industrial Revolution.

r003.rationale: It describes machines helping people work more effectively, but does not state that people generally redirect time freed by automation toward more constructive activities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fear comes partly from imagining automation as an all-or-nothing proposition: eventually machines will do everything, and there won’t be anything left for us to do. But robotics gives you a very different perspective. You discover how difficult it is to do things that humans do effortlessly, particularly in an unpredictable physical environment.

That doesn’t mean automation won’t have a profound effect on work. It will, and we need to take the disruption seriously. But I’m more interested in how people and machines can complement one another. Machines have certain strengths, and humans bring judgment, context, and an ability to adapt. The question is how we design systems that bring those strengths together, and how we make sure the benefits are shared.

r001.rationale: The response questions the idea that machines will eventually do everything and notes how difficult physical tasks are to automate, but it does not state that a fully automated world is not imminent.
